title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP, also known as Hamman–Rich syndrome) is an acute, rapidly progressive idiopathic pulmonary disease that often leads to fulminant respiratory failure and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). [1] AIP can be distinguished clinically from other types of interstitial pneumonia by the rapid onset of respiratory failure in a patient without preexisting lung disease. [2] Louis Hamman and Arnold Rich first described AIP in 1935 as a fulminating diffuse interstitial fibrosis of the lungs. [3] In 1986, Katzenstein introduced the term AIP, differentiating it from the group of chronic interstitial pneumonias. [4] [5] The American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society classify AIP as a major idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, compared with other rare or unclassified idiopathic interstitial pneumonias. [1]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP) has no known etiology.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: The mean age of patients with AIP is approximately 55 years. There is no sex predilection. [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP) is thought to be triggered by an unknown insult to the alveolar epithelium, leading to activation of the inflammatory cascade, followed by fibroblastic activity in the late stage. [6]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP) has the histopathological pattern of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), which is indistinguishable from that found in ARDS. [1] [4] [7] The histologic description depends on the timing of the biopsy. The early phase (within a week of the initial tissue injury) is exudative, characterized by interstitial and alveolar edema. Next, a late phase, also called the organizing phase, shows fibroblastic proliferation and hyperplasia of type II pneumocytes. [2] [4] [7]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Symptoms usually start with a viral-like prodrome followed by shortness of breath, cough, and fever, and progress rapidly to acute respiratory distress. The physical examination is nonspecific with hypoxia, tachypnea, and bilateral diffuse crackles. Many patients are severely hypoxemic and require mechanical ventilation. [5] [6] [7] [9] A detailed history with a comprehensive medical examination is essential to investigate other causes of acute DAD, as noted below, under differential diagnosis.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Patients with acute interstitial pneumonia are at risk of rapid respiratory decompensation, and vital signs should be monitored closely. Arterial blood gases can identify the severity of hypoxemia and the need for mechanical ventilation. Chest radiograph usually shows a pattern similar to ARDS, with bilateral diffuse airspace opacities. Therefore, ruling out cardiac causes of pulmonary edema is essential. Echocardiography is needed to rule out underlying cardiomyopathy or valvular dysfunction. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is usually abnormal in the first 12 hours, showing diffuse or patchy ground-glass opacities and air-space consolidation. HRCT findings correlate with the different phases of DAD. [8] [10] [11] [12] CT findings can also show traction bronchiectasis, indicating progression from the exudative phase to the proliferative fibrotic phase. [11]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Laboratory testing should include screening for autoimmune and connective tissue diseases associated with lung disease, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, and Sjögren disease. [13] Microbiologic testing should include blood and sputum cultures. Influenza screening is important, as well as serology for atypical organisms and fungi. Legionella spp are atypical organisms that can be detected with a urine antigen test. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage is needed to exclude diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, eosinophilia, or malignant infiltrates. In acute interstitial pneumonia, bronchoalveolar lavage results are usually nonspecific, with neutrophilia and scattered atypical type II pneumocytes. [14] Bronchoscopy also helps obtain respiratory samples for culture when sputum production is absent. The sample should be sent for cell count and cytology, cultures, and Pneumocystis jirovecii immunofluorescence.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: If this evaluation does not achieve an alternative diagnosis, lung biopsy may be indicated. Lung biopsy might also reveal different etiologies, including caseating granulomas (tuberculosis), noncaseating granulomas (sarcoidosis), necrosis (vasculitis), abscesses, or viral inclusions. Acute interstitial pneumonia is an idiopathic disease. After excluding other causes of ARDS, pathologic confirmation of idiopathic DAD is necessary to establish the diagnosis.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: There is no evidence-based treatment for AIP. [1] Management is largely based on supportive care. Adequate oxygenation is often not achievable without mechanical ventilation. [9] [15] Similar to ARDS, arterial blood gases can identify the severity of respiratory distress based on the Berlin Criteria (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen to fraction of inspired oxygen [PaO 2: FiO 2 ]). [16] [17] Ventilator management primarily focuses on low-tidal-volume ventilation and other advanced ventilator modalities, such as those used in ARDS. [16] [17] Broad-spectrum antibiotics are recommended initially until an infectious etiology is excluded.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Although corticosteroid therapy is usually started empirically, it has no clear benefit in AIP. In findings from a case series of 29 patients with AIP, 12 patients survived. Survival was 45% in patients who received corticosteroids, compared with 33% in those who did not. [7] However, the mortality was 100% in findings from a different case series of 9 patients who all received intravenous methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg 4 times a day. [15] Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and lung transplant should be considered for appropriate candidates if conventional therapy is ineffective. [9] [15] [18]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnosis of acute interstitial pneumonia includes: Other causes of interstitial pneumonia, such as cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, acute eosinophilic pneumonia, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis Acute exacerbation of underlying interstitial lung disease or pulmonary exacerbation of a connective tissue disease Acute heart failure Infections Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Drug-induced lung injury Radiation-induced lung injury

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: The mortality rate is greater than 50% at initial presentation or within 6 months after onset. [1] [4] [5] [7] [9] [15] Among survivors, recurrence and development of chronic interstitial lung disease have been reported. [9]

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should be educated on the following key points: Acute interstitial pneumonia is a disease of unclear etiology, which limits prevention strategies and the ability to predict its onset. Initial symptoms are nonspecific and can resemble other respiratory diseases. Patients should seek medical advice early, before respiratory deterioration. There is no specific test for acute interstitial pneumonia, and the only way to confirm it is a lung biopsy. There is no specific medication to treat acute interstitial pneumonia. Management is generally supportive.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: The following are clinical pearls regarding AIP: AIP is diagnosed after excluding other causes of acute diffuse alveolar damage. There is no specific treatment for AIP. Management is mostly supportive. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started until an infectious etiology is excluded. A lung-protective strategy should be implemented. Treatment with corticosteroids has no clear benefit in AIP. Mortality is high, and lung transplant should be considered for appropriate candidates. AIP usually presents similarly to ARDS.

title: Acute Interstitial Pneumonia(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Acute interstitial pneumonia is an uncommon disease that presents acutely and progresses rapidly with a high mortality rate. Diagnosis is complex and requires an interdisciplinary team, including pulmonology, radiology, and pathology. Proper communication and coordination between members of the health care team can expedite the diagnostic process and, therefore, initiate supportive care earlier. The primary team should also be aware of the possible complications that may arise during the acute illness. Further research is needed to clarify the initial triggers and progression of the disease to improve outcomes.
